Baskets & Weaving

7 Common Leaf Weaving Mistakes and How to Fix Them

Loose bases, cracked folds and wobbly rims all trace back to the same few causes. Here are the seven mistakes I see most, and the fix for each one.

9 April 2025 ME By Maya Ellis 8 min read 884 words
Share

On this page

  1. Mistake 1: Weaving with Leaves That Have Dried Out
  2. Mistake 2: Tension That Drifts From Row to Row
  3. Mistake 3: A Base That Cups Instead of Lying Flat
  4. Mistake 4: Leaves Cracking at the Fold

In short

Loose bases, cracked folds and wobbly rims all trace back to the same few causes. Here are the seven mistakes I see most, and the fix for each one.

Every woven basket that failed, failed for one of a small number of reasons. After teaching this craft for years, I can usually spot the cause within a minute of picking up a beginner basket. It is almost never the pattern and almost never a lack of talent.

Here are the seven mistakes I see most often, what each one looks like, and the fix. Most take minutes to correct and save hours of frustration, and all of them are easier to spot than you would think once you know what to look for.

The good news is that all seven mistakes are recoverable. Leaf is forgiving. You can undo a row, dampen it, and reweave without leaving a mark, as long as you catch the problem within a day or two. The only real cost is time, and fixing a problem early costs far less than finishing a basket you are unhappy with. I have undone entire bases and reworked them in under half an hour; it feels dramatic at the time and is forgotten the moment the basket is finished.

Mistake 1: Weaving with Leaves That Have Dried Out

Dry leaves crack at every fold and refuse to lie flat. If a strip snaps when you bend it back on itself, it is too dry. Soak the strips in cool water for fifteen to twenty minutes, then pat them dry with a cloth. Do not leave them in the water for hours, though; over-soaked leaf turns limp and loses the springiness that makes a weave hold. Work with a spray bottle beside you and mist the weave every so often on a hot day. The fix is simple, and it prevents the two mistakes that follow. Keep the water bowl covered with a cloth so leaf does not soak up dust and grit from the air.

Mistake 2: Tension That Drifts From Row to Row

Uneven tension is the single most common flaw. It happens when you pull the first rows tight and then relax as you get bored or tired. The basket bulges in the middle and pinches at the rim. The fix is to weave in short bursts and check the wall every three rows by pressing it flat on the table. If it wobbles, undo back to where the tension was even. Consistency matters more than tightness; a uniformly loose basket looks far better than a patchy one. Aim for the same gentle resistance on every pass, as if you were tightening a shoelace rather than hauling on a rope.

  1. Press the wall flat after every third row to catch drift early.
  2. Weave for twenty minutes, then stop and check rather than pushing on.
  3. Keep the working strip damp so it does not stiffen and pull unevenly.
  4. Compare the two sides of the basket with your hands, not just your eyes.
  5. Count your rows on both sides; a difference of one row shows as a lopsided rim.

Mistake 3: A Base That Cups Instead of Lying Flat

A cupped base means the first rows were pulled too tight, drawing the centre upwards. Turn the base over and press it flat under a heavy book for twenty minutes while it is still slightly damp. If it springs back, undo the outermost two rows and reweave them more loosely. A base that domes downwards instead is the opposite fault: you wove too loosely in the middle. In that case, dampen it and reweave the centre rows a little tighter. The base sets the whole basket, so it is worth getting right before you build the walls.

Mistake 4: Leaves Cracking at the Fold

Cracks appear when you fold across the leaf vein instead of along it. The vein is the leaf's hinge; folding against it splits the fibres. Always orient strips so the vein runs the length of the fold, and you will almost never see a crack again. If one does appear, do not panic. Dampen the strip, overlap the cracked section with a fresh strip, and weave both in for a few rows so the join is hidden inside the wall. A well-hidden repair is invisible in a finished basket.

MistakeWhat it looks likeThe fix
Mistake 5: Rushing the rimA wavy, uneven top edge that will not sit flat.Undo the last two rows and re-tuck one upright at a time.
Mistake 6: Weaving too looselyDaylight visible through the wall and a floppy feel.Reweave the next row snug against the last, then press flat.
Mistake 7: Ignoring the grainStrips that twist and refuse to lie flat.Fold along the vein, never across it, and dampen before folding.

Never leave a half-finished basket in direct sun. It dries unevenly and the rim sets crooked, which is the hardest fault of all to correct later. Cover it with a damp cloth and put it in the shade if you have to stop mid-weave.

Helpful Tips

  • Undo a bad row immediately; leaf remembers a crease for only a few minutes.
  • Keep a bowl of water and a cloth within reach the whole time you weave.
  • Weave in daylight. Tension problems are almost invisible under warm indoor light.
  • Finish a small basket before starting a large one; momentum matters more than ambition.

Learn the weave properly, once.

Frequently asked questions

Why is my basket loose and floppy?

Almost always uneven tension. Pull each new row snug against the last and check the wall every three rows, undoing back to where it was even.

Can I fix a basket after it has dried?

Partly. Mist the area with water, wait five minutes for it to soften, then reweave. Fully cured baskets hold their shape but folds can still be eased.

Do I need to soak leaves before weaving?

Fresh leaves usually do not need it. Leaves more than a day old should soak for fifteen to twenty minutes so they fold without cracking.

What is the most common beginner mistake?

Uneven tension, followed closely by weaving with leaves that are too dry. Fix both and your baskets improve immediately.
